$schemaNote: Ownership catalog for docs/architecture-split-plan.md. Machine-readable source of truth enforced by backend/RealEstateEval.Architecture.Tests. 'owner' is the approved write owner of the table; 'contexts' names the EF DbContext(s) that hold its write path today. Phase 1 moves a table's write path from ApplicationDbContext to its owner context one vertical slice at a time; a table may not appear in a context that is not listed here.

contexts.name: PlatformDbContext

contexts.name: FailuresDbContext

After the Phase 4 cutover those D2 tables live on the dedicated operations database, still in the case_study schema until a later relocate.

contexts.name: FinancialDbContext
contexts.note: Phase 1 extraction order, step 4. financial schema plus D1 inspector-fee tables still physically named in case_study. After the Phase 4 cutover those D1 tables live on the dedicated financial database, still in the case_study schema until a later relocate.

contexts.name: CaseStudyDbContext
contexts.note: Phase 1 extraction order, step 4. Case Study–owned case_study tables only (not D1 inspector fees, not D2 operations tasks).

contexts.name: MessagingDbContext
contexts.note: Phase 1 extraction order, step 5. Platform-owned notifications/push (D3) and migration stream for messaging tables. Outbox/inbox also mapped so Platform writes share one SaveChanges. After the Phase 4 cutover Case Study drains the dedicated messaging database via MessagingDbContext; Valuation drains its dedicated outbox from the valuation database (D5).

decisions.question: Who owns inspector-fee ledgers, fee transitions, and disbursement batches?
decisions.rationale: Accrual, discount, exclusion, batching and disbursement are financial lifecycle states, and financial reporting plus engineering billing already read the ledger. The rows stay in the case_study schema: ownership is behavioural now, relocation is a Phase 4 data migration.
decisions.note: Rows live in case_study but the accrual/disbursement lifecycle is financial. Moving the tables is a data migration, so ownership must be decided before any context takes the write path.

decisions.question: Who owns operations tasks, their sequences, and court-visit fee charge creation?
decisions.outcome: operations owns OperationsTasks and OperationsTaskSequences; financial owns CourtVisitFeeCharges
decisions.rationale: The task lifecycle (court visits, letters, key handover) is operations work; the charge it produces is a financial artefact priced and collected by Financial. Charge creation moves behind a Financial command in Phase 3; the OperationsTasks rows stay in the case_study schema until Phase 4.
decisions.note: OperationsTasks/OperationsTaskSequences live in case_study and are written by OperationsTaskService on the Operations host; the same service writes financial.CourtVisitFeeCharges.

decisions.question: Who owns the notification inbox rows and how are recipients resolved?
decisions.outcome: platform owns messaging.UserNotifications; non-owners request notifications through the outbox; real-time push is emitted from the Platform transaction
decisions.rationale: Platform already exposes the list/mutation endpoints and PlatformNotificationRequestService already routes non-owner writes through notification.users.requested.v1. Recipient resolution stays a Platform concern and becomes a Platform-owned projection or an Identity/Case Study owner contract in Phase 3; NotificationRecipientResolver's direct identity/case_study reads are the adapter to remove.
decisions.note: Ownership is settled; the table moves to a Platform-owned messaging context in Phase 1 extraction step 5, not in step 1.

decisions.question: Who owns document-reference counters?
decisions.rationale: The counter is the correspondence-numbering sequence of the case-study document set, not a financial artefact; engineering billing is one consumer of it. Financial obtains numbers through a Case Study command in Phase 3 instead of incrementing the row itself.
decisions.note: Counter rows live in case_study and are consumed by engineering billing document numbering.

decisions.question: What is the service-local shape of the messaging outbox/inbox once producers and consumers are separated?
decisions.rationale: Each producing context maps messaging.OutboxMessages and owns only the rows it inserts, so a business write and its event stay in one SaveChanges. Each consuming context maps messaging.ProcessedIntegrationEvents and owns the rows carrying its own Consumer value. The single Case Study dispatcher stays until the messaging slice; splitting dispatch is Phase 1 extraction step 5, and per-service claim isolation is a Phase 4 prerequisite.
decisions.note: Consequence: messaging.OutboxMessages and messaging.ProcessedIntegrationEvents are the only tables allowed in more than one context. Their ownershipModel records that.

decisions.question: Which production-only SQL clients, BI jobs, database roles, and cross-schema database objects read these tables?
decisions.outcome: not discoverable from this repository; does not block Phase 1, remains a hard gate for Phase 3 grant changes and Phase 4 data movement
decisions.rationale: Phase 1 changes only which EF context holds a write path. It renames no table, moves no row, changes no grant and emits no DDL, so an unknown external reader cannot be broken by it. The inventory is still required before schema-limited roles are granted (Phase 3) and is a stop condition for physical data movement (Phase 4).
decisions.note: Judgment call recorded on approval: the ownership decisions D1-D5 were approved without it; the operations deliverable is still outstanding and is listed in the remaining gate.

decisions.question: Where does the shared audit ledger live, and who may write it?
decisions.outcome: dedicated audit schema holding one append-only table; rows owned per producer
decisions.rationale: Identity, platform and case-study all append audit rows in the same transaction as the change they record, so the ledger cannot belong to a single owner's schema without granting every writer that owner's whole schema — putting courts, regions and configuration within reach of the Identity service, which otherwise sees only identity. A schema containing this one table keeps the central query surface intact while letting Phase 3 grant INSERT on the ledger alone. Splitting into one table per context was rejected: it fragments the central audit view and its pagination for no boundary gain, since rows are already per-producer.
decisions.note: Consequence: audit.AuditLogs is mapped by every writing context. PlatformDbContext creates and shapes it; the others exclude it from migrations. UPDATE and DELETE are rejected by a database trigger, so append-only holds even for a direct SQL client.
